quotes.text: Chaos engineering is a practical method. You inject real controlled failures into your system and observe how it reacts. This doesn't happen in a lab or a simulation. It happens on your actual resources.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: Here's the thing, chaos engineering is not random destruction. It's not a developer walking into the server room and pulling cables for fun. It's scientific, repeatable, and safety constrained.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: Start small and start in a non-production environment. Run your first experiments in dev or staging, test with a single VM and a single fault, and validate that your monitoring works
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical safety recommendation for getting started.

quotes.text: The key idea across all three approaches is that chaos engineering is not a one-time test. You don't run one experiment, declare your system resilient, and move on.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Frames resilience as a continuous practice.

quotes.text: Load testing tells you if your system can handle the traffic. Chaos engineering tells you if it can survive the failures.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Memorable contrast between two resilience practices.

takeaways: Chaos engineering injects real, controlled failures to test a hypothesis about how your system survives them.
Azure Chaos Studio runs service-direct and agent-based faults through experiments built from targets, steps, branches and actions.
Start small in non-production, use managed identities and fault enablement as safety nets, and make experiments a continuous practice.
hook: Traditional tests assume everything works, but production rarely does. In this episode Mirko Peters explains Azure Chaos Studio for cloud architects, DevOps engineers and SREs, showing how controlled failure experiments reveal weaknesses before your customers do.
